# blue

> blue is a general-purpose language with a Ruby/Elixir surface that parses to a tatara-lisp tree and runs on a Rust runtime. It has one formatting, rigor where you write it, and most of its vocabulary in packages called bidamas.

---

Source: `docs/introduction.md`

# blue

```text
████  blue          nord7 → nord8 → nord9 → nord10
────────────────────    teal   cyan   light  deep blue
a Ruby/Elixir surface on tatara-lisp and Rust
```

**blue** is the pleme-io language. You write it like Ruby or Elixir. It
parses to a [tatara-lisp](https://github.com/pleme-io/tatara-lisp) tree,
macros rewrite that tree, and a Rust runtime runs it, not the BEAM. Each
thing has one spelling, and the formatter writes it. Rigor is your choice:
declare nothing and a program is dynamic and fast; annotate one function and
that function is checked. The standard library is a set of packages called
bidamas, and one `Bluefile` says how a project is built, tested, rendered and
shipped.

The philosophy is two axes
([`theory/BLUE.md`](https://github.com/pleme-io/theory/blob/main/BLUE.md) §0).
**Form has no choices:** there is one short, distinct way to write each
thing, every larger form is built from smaller ones, and every tool and gate
enforces it. **Rigor has every choice:** a program is as strict as you write
it, where you write it, and pays for nothing else.

## The blueshift

The blueshift is how far a program has moved from dynamic toward checked.
You move it one definition at a time. Here `add` has no annotation, so
nothing analyses it. `fact` is annotated, so the checker proves it:

```blue file=shift.b
def add(a, b)
  a + b
end

def fact(n: Int) -> Int
  if n < 2
    1
  else
    n * fact(n - 1)
  end
end
```

`blue check` prints what the check cost, so the claim is a measurement:

```console
$ blue check shift.b
typed declarations: 1
nodes analysed:     11
seams:              0
names resolved:     11
waived:             0
```

`blue shift` names the rung the file stands on and what holds it back:

```console
$ blue shift shift.b
██░░ annotated  (1/2 typed, 11 nodes analysed)
some declarations are typed; untyped ones are unchecked

  · untyped declaration      `add` has no annotation — annotate it to shift further
  → type annotation          `fact` is annotated, so it is checked
```

The mark is a blueshift too: four solid cells walk Nord's Frost band toward
blue. A blueshift is a shift in colour, so the mark shifts colour. It names
each colour by ANSI slot, never by hex, so it renders in your Nord and
follows you when you retheme.

## Commands

| Command | |
|---|---|
| `blue FILE ARGS` | run a program as a script: quiet, every argument after the file reaches `argv` |
| `blue run FILE` | parse, check, erase and run, then print the final value |
| `blue test FILE` | check the file, then run its `test` blocks and its doctests |
| `blue fmt FILE [--check\|--write]` | the one formatting |
| `blue check FILE` | every rule, and what the type checker did |
| `blue shift FILE` | the blueshift: how far the file is checked, and what holds it back |
| `blue doc NAME` | what a name is: signature, doc line, tier and an example |
| `blue new NAME` | a project; `--bidama NAME` a package; `--script NAME.b` a script |
| `blue ast FILE` / `blue erase FILE` | the tree with and without annotations |
| `blue lock DIR` | evaluate a `Bluefile` into `Bluefile.lock` |
| `blue reference` | the language reference, as JSON |
| `blue lsp` | the language server over stdio |
| `blue repl` / `blue eval EXPR` | an evaluation session at the terminal, or one expression |
| `blue banner` | the wordmark |

## What is here

Macros with **bounded expansion**: a runaway macro is a typed error that
names the macro, not a dead compiler. OTP-style **supervision** with private
per-process environments and copy-on-send. A **test framework** whose
failures print the expression as blue source, and **doctests** in every
`@doc`. A **package manager** whose manifest is itself a blue program. A
**WASM** target that runs the whole language with zero host imports.

## What is not

blue states its gaps plainly, because a language's honest gaps matter more
than its claims:

- **No per-process GC heap.** Processes have private environments and
  messages are deep-copied, but reclamation is `Arc` refcounting. There is no
  independent per-process collection pause.
- **Not self-hosted.** The toolchain is Rust. `spec/*.b` is blue specifying
  blue, which is the specification axis only.
- **Nothing fetches.** Dependency resolution is real; there is no registry
  client.
- **The formatter refuses a comment it cannot place.** It keeps comments
  before and after a top-level form. It refuses a comment inside an
  expression rather than drop it.

The full tier ledger, every row marked SHIPPED or ABSENT, is
[`theory/BLUE.md`](https://github.com/pleme-io/theory/blob/main/BLUE.md) §V.26.

## Theming

Colours come from [irodori](https://github.com/pleme-io/irodori), the fleet's
Nord palette. blue carries no hex of its own. `nord10` (`#5E81AC`, deep frost
blue) is its identity, and `nord8` frost cyan stays the fleet's shared
interaction colour: identity and interaction are different roles.

## Building blue

```console host
$ nix build .#blue
$ nix flake check
$ cargo test --workspace
```

`nix build` is hermetic. `nix flake check` runs every gate the root
`Bluefile` declares. Changing blue itself starts at [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md).

MIT.

---

Source: `docs/tutorial/install.md`

# Install blue

You need [Nix](https://nixos.org) with flakes turned on. Install blue into
your profile:

```console host
$ nix profile install github:pleme-io/blue
```

To try blue without installing it, put `nix run github:pleme-io/blue --` in
front of each command below.

Ask blue for a value:

```console
$ blue eval '1 + 2'
3
```

Write a file called `hello.b`:

```blue file=hello.b
write_stdout(unlines(["Olá, mundo!"]))
```

Run it:

```console
$ blue hello.b
Olá, mundo!
```

That is a whole blue program. The next tutorial, [a first script](docs/tutorial/first-script.md),
gives it arguments.

---

Source: `docs/tutorial/first-script.md`

# A first script

A script is one file that runs from the command line. It needs no project
and no configuration.

Write `greet.b`:

```blue file=greet.b
#!/usr/bin/env blue
def greeting(who)
  "hello, #{who}"
end

write_stdout(unlines([greeting(argv_get(0, "world"))]))
```

`argv_get(0, "world")` reads the first argument, or `"world"` when there is
none. Run the script with and without one:

```console
$ blue greet.b
hello, world
$ blue greet.b ryn
hello, ryn
```

The first line is a shebang. After `chmod +x greet.b`, the script also runs as
`./greet.b ryn`.

blue writes one formatting. Ask it whether the file is in that form:

```console
$ blue fmt --check greet.b
```

No output means yes. `blue fmt --write` puts a file into the form.

`blue new --script` starts a script for you, already executable and already
formatted:

```console
$ blue new --script tool.b
created tool.b, executable
run it   ./tool.b  (or blue tool.b)
$ blue tool.b a b
hello, a (2 argument(s))
```

A script can `use` every standard bidama with no setup. When a script
outgrows one file, it becomes [a first program](docs/tutorial/first-program.md).

---

Source: `docs/tutorial/first-program.md`

# A first program

A program is a project: a `Bluefile` that says how it is built, a `main.b`
that runs it, and its code in a bidama of its own. `blue new` writes one that
passes its tests as written:

```console
$ blue new tally
created tally/: Bluefile, Bluefile.lock, flake.nix, main.b, bidamas/tally/
run it   blue tally/main.b
test it  blue test tally/bidamas/tally/tally.b
$ cd tally
$ blue main.b ryn
hello, ryn
```

Now make it count words. Replace `bidamas/tally/tally.b` with this:

```blue file=bidamas/tally/tally.b
use("retsu", [:size])

def words(text)
  filter((w) -> w != "", split(text, " "))
end

def tally(text)
  size(words(text))
end

def main(args)
  write_stdout(unlines([to_s(tally(join(args, " ")))]))
end

test "words are what the spaces separate"
  assert tally("one two  three") == 3
end

test "an empty text has no words"
  assert tally("") == 0
end
```

Run the tests. `blue test` checks the file first, then runs each `test`
block:

```console
$ blue test bidamas/tally/tally.b
2 test(s): 2 passed, 0 failed
```

Run the program:

```console
$ blue main.b the quick brown fox
4
```

`main.b` stayed the same: it calls `main(argv)` from the `tally` bidama. Next,
[a first bidama](docs/tutorial/first-bidama.md) documents a package so others can use it.

---

Source: `docs/tutorial/first-bidama.md`

# A first bidama

A bidama is a blue package. It documents itself: a `@moduledoc` says what
the package is for, and a `@doc` above each definition says what it does,
with an example that `blue test` runs.

Start a program, then a second bidama beside its own:

```console
$ blue new shelf
created shelf/: Bluefile, Bluefile.lock, flake.nix, main.b, bidamas/shelf/
run it   blue shelf/main.b
test it  blue test shelf/bidamas/shelf/shelf.b
$ cd shelf/bidamas
$ blue new --bidama prose
created prose/: Bluefile, Bluefile.lock, prose.b
test it  blue test prose/prose.b
$ cd ..
```

Replace `bidamas/prose/prose.b` with a documented package:

```blue file=bidamas/prose/prose.b
@moduledoc """
prose: split text into words and count them.

    count_words("a b") #=> 2
"""

use("retsu", [:size])

@doc """
words: The words of a text: the runs of characters between spaces.

    words(" a  b ") #=> ["a", "b"]
"""
def words(text)
  filter((w) -> w != "", split(text, " "))
end

@doc """
count_words: How many words a text holds.

    count_words("the quick brown fox") #=> 4
"""
def count_words(text)
  size(words(text))
end

test "an empty text has no words"
  assert count_words("") == 0
end
```

Each `expr #=> value` line in a doc is a doctest. `blue test` runs them with
the `test` blocks:

```console
$ blue test bidamas/prose/prose.b
4 test(s): 4 passed, 0 failed
```

`blue doc` shows a definition as a reader sees it:

```console
$ BLUE_PATH=bidamas blue doc prose::count_words
prose::count_words(text)
  bidama prose · tier: qualified
  count_words: How many words a text holds.
  
      count_words("the quick brown fox") #=> 4
  · signature `def count_words(text)` · rung dynamic
  example (test "an empty text has no words"):
    assert count_words("") == 0
```

Now use the package from the program. Replace `bidamas/shelf/shelf.b`:

```blue file=bidamas/shelf/shelf.b
use("prose", [:count_words])

def main(args)
  write_stdout(unlines(["#{count_words(join(args, " "))} words"]))
end

test "the program counts its arguments' words"
  assert count_words("a b c") == 3
end
```

A bidama's `Bluefile` and lock record the packages its files use. `shelf`
now uses `prose` and no longer uses `retsu`, so the check refuses the old
lock and names its fixer. Run it, then run the program:

```console
$ blue check --fix bidamas/shelf/shelf.b
$ blue main.b one two three
3 words
```

The next tutorial, [a first service](docs/tutorial/first-service.md), declares a service
in the `Bluefile`.

---

Source: `docs/tutorial/first-service.md`

# A first service

A service is one declaration and one program. The declaration names what the
service needs; blue renders the chart, the settings schema, the image and
the checks from it. This tutorial builds a small copy of
[ola-mundo](https://github.com/pleme-io/ola-mundo), the reference blue service.

Make a directory for the service, and declare it in a `Bluefile`:

```console
$ mkdir hello
$ cd hello
```

```blue file=Bluefile
package("hello", "0.1.0")

service(
  "hello",
  {
    program: "hello.b",
    repository: "ghcr.io/example/hello",
    port: 8080,
    config: {greeting: "Olá", subject: "mundo"}
  }
)

check("hello", "hello.b")
```

The program answers `GET /`. `settei` reads the settings the declaration
gives it, and `kyuuji` serves HTTP:

```blue file=hello.b
use("kyuuji")
use("settei")

def greeting(s, who)
  subject = if who == nil or who == ""
    settei::setting(s, "subject")
  else
    who
  end
  "#{settei::setting(s, "greeting")}, #{subject}!"
end

def handle(s, req)
  if get(req, :method) == "GET" and get(req, :path) == "/"
    kyuuji::text(200, unlines([greeting(s, kyuuji::query_param(req, "who"))]))
  else
    kyuuji::not_found(req)
  end
end

if settei::serving?
  s = settei::current
  kyuuji::serve_settings(s, (req) -> handle(s, req))
end

def settings()
  {"greeting" => "Olá", "subject" => "mundo"}
end

test "the root greets the configured subject"
  r = handle(settings, kyuuji::request("GET", "/", ""))
  assert get(r, :status) == 200
  assert get(r, :body) == unlines(["Olá, mundo!"])
end

test "any other path is not found"
  assert get(handle(settings, kyuuji::request("GET", "/x", "")), :status) ==
    404
end
```

The handler is a function from a request to a response, so the tests call
it directly. Lock the declaration and run the tests:

```console
$ blue lock .
./Bluefile.lock: 0 source(s) pinned
$ blue test hello.b
2 test(s): 2 passed, 0 failed
```

The `haibi` bidama renders the declaration into everything that ships the
service. This program lists the files it would write:

```blue file=../show.b
use("haibi", [:files])
use("retsu", [:first])

m = get(json_read(read_file("hello/Bluefile.lock")), "manifest")
spec = get(get(m, "services"), "hello")
paths = map(first, files("hello", get(m, "version"), spec))
write_stdout(unlines(sort_keyed((p) -> p, paths)))
```

```console
$ cd ..
$ blue show.b
chart/Chart.yaml
chart/files/dashboard.json
chart/templates/NOTES.txt
chart/templates/dashboard.yaml
chart/templates/deployment.yaml
chart/templates/service.yaml
chart/templates/serviceaccount.yaml
chart/templates/slo-rules.yaml
chart/values.schema.json
chart/values.yaml
config/hello.schema.json
config/hello.yaml
```

A real service adds a one-line `flake.nix` (`blue.lib.project { src = ./.; }`,
as ola-mundo has). Then nix builds the image and runs every check:

```console host
$ nix flake check
```

The [how-to guides](docs/howto/test-and-doctest.md) each do one task from
here.

---

Source: `docs/howto/test-and-doctest.md`

# Write a test and a doctest

Put a `test` block beside the code it tests, in the same file. `assert`
fails the test when its expression is false:

```blue file=math.b
@doc """
double: Twice a number.

    double(21) #=> 42
"""
def double(n)
  n * 2
end

test "double of zero is zero"
  assert double(0) == 0
end

test "double of a negative stays negative"
  assert double(-3) == -6
end
```

The `#=>` line in the `@doc` is a doctest: `blue test` runs it beside the
`test` blocks.

```console
$ blue test math.b
3 test(s): 3 passed, 0 failed
```

Run only the tests whose name holds a word:

```console
$ blue test --filter negative math.b
1 test(s): 1 passed, 0 failed
```

A failure prints the expression as you wrote it, with both sides:

```blue file=wrong.b
test "two and two"
  assert 2 + 2 == 5
end
```

```console fails
$ blue test wrong.b
FAIL two and two
  assert 2 + 2 == 5
```

`blue test DIR` runs every file under a directory that holds a test, in
parallel.

---

Source: `docs/howto/climb-the-blueshift.md`

# Climb the blueshift

`blue shift` names the rung a file stands on: dynamic, annotated, checked or
restricted. You climb by annotating definitions.

Start with a file that declares nothing:

```blue file=area.b
def area(w, h)
  w * h
end

def square(s)
  area(s, s)
end
```

```console
$ blue shift area.b
█░░░ dynamic  (0/2 typed, 0 nodes analysed)
no annotations — no analysis runs, and nothing is checked

  · untyped declaration      `area` has no annotation — annotate it to shift further
  · untyped declaration      `square` has no annotation — annotate it to shift further
```

Annotate `area`. The file moves up one rung, and `blue shift` names what
still holds it back:

```blue file=area.b
def area(w: Int, h: Int) -> Int
  w * h
end

def square(s)
  area(s, s)
end
```

```console
$ blue shift area.b
██░░ annotated  (1/2 typed, 3 nodes analysed)
some declarations are typed; untyped ones are unchecked

  → type annotation          `area` is annotated, so it is checked
  · untyped declaration      `square` has no annotation — annotate it to shift further
```

Annotate `square` too, and every declaration is checked:

```blue file=area.b
def area(w: Int, h: Int) -> Int
  w * h
end

def square(s: Int) -> Int
  area(s, s)
end
```

```console
$ blue shift area.b
███░ checked  (2/2 typed, 6 nodes analysed)
every declaration is typed, so the whole file is checked

  → type annotation          `area` is annotated, so it is checked
  → type annotation          `square` is annotated, so it is checked
```

A wrong annotation is now an error before the program runs:

```blue file=bad.b
def half(n: Int) -> Int
  "half"
end
```

```console fails
$ blue check bad.b
error[B0003]: `half` declares it returns Int, but its body produces Str
```

The `pleme-io/actions/blue-shift` action holds a project to a floor rung in
CI.

---

Source: `docs/howto/declare-access.md`

# Declare what a program may touch

A program that runs with no flag may reach every host capability. `--allow`
holds a run to the ones you name: `none`, `host`, or any of `process`,
`filesystem`, `environment`, `clock`, `network` and `entropy`.

Here is a program that reads a file:

```blue file=peek.b
write_stdout(read_file("note.txt"))
```

```blue file=note.txt
a note
```

With `--allow none`, blue refuses it before it runs, and names the flag that
grants it:

```console fails
$ blue run --allow none --quiet peek.b
refused: `read_file` reaches the host (filesystem)
```

Grant exactly what it needs:

```console
$ blue run --allow filesystem --quiet peek.b
a note
```

A script states its capabilities in its shebang, so `./peek.b` carries them
with it:

```blue file=peek2.b
#!/usr/bin/env -S blue --allow filesystem
write_stdout(read_file("note.txt"))
```

Every Rust guarantee, the blue gate that matches it and its off switch are in
[SAFETY.md](docs/SAFETY.md). One access declaration for a whole service, in its
`service(...)` entry, is designed in
[SERVICE-ACCESS.md](docs/SERVICE-ACCESS.md) and not built yet.

---

Source: `docs/howto/write-an-action.md`

# Write an action

A pleme-io action keeps its logic in a `run.b`. The `koutei` bidama is that
file's side of the step: it reads the `INPUT_*` variables, writes outputs and
the step summary, and fails the step.

Write `run.b`:

```blue file=run.b
use("koutei", [:fail, :input_or, :output])

who = input_or("who", "world")
if who == "nobody"
  fail("there is nobody to greet")
end
output("greeting", "hello, #{who}")
```

Run it the way the runner does: inputs as `INPUT_*` variables, outputs to the
file `GITHUB_OUTPUT` names.

```console
$ INPUT_WHO=ryn GITHUB_OUTPUT=out.txt blue run --quiet run.b
$ cat out.txt
greeting<<KOUTEI_EOF
hello, ryn
KOUTEI_EOF
```

With no `GITHUB_OUTPUT`, `koutei` prints the record, so a local run shows it:

```console
$ blue run --quiet run.b
greeting<<KOUTEI_EOF
hello, world
KOUTEI_EOF
```

A refused input fails the step with an error annotation:

```console fails
$ INPUT_WHO=nobody blue run --quiet run.b
::error::there is nobody to greet
```

The `action.yml` beside it passes the inputs and runs the file:

```yaml
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - shell: bash
      env:
        INPUT_WHO: ${{ inputs.who }}
      run: blue run --quiet "${{ github.action_path }}/run.b"
```

`pleme-io/actions/blue-shift` is a complete example.

---

Source: `docs/howto/publish-a-bidama.md`

# Publish a bidama

A bidama is reachable when it sits under a `packages` root: a directory of
packages, each with its own `Bluefile`. A project finds packages through its
own `packages(...)` roots, then `BLUE_PATH`, then the distribution compiled
into `blue`.

Make a library of one package:

```console
$ mkdir lib
$ cd lib
$ blue new --bidama greet
created greet/: Bluefile, Bluefile.lock, greet.b
test it  blue test greet/greet.b
$ cd ..
```

Another project reaches it with `BLUE_PATH`:

```blue file=app.b
use("greet", [:greeting])

write_stdout(unlines([greeting(["ryn"])]))
```

```console
$ BLUE_PATH=lib blue app.b
hello, ryn
```

A project publishes itself with `registry(...)` entries in its `Bluefile`.
Each entry is one backend. The backend renders from the `Bluefile` and its
lock, which stay the truth. `package`'s third argument sets visibility once:

```blue file=lib/Bluefile
package("greetings", "0.1.0", :public)

packages(".")
registry(:sui, {outputs: ["default"]})
```

```console
$ cd lib
$ blue lock .
./Bluefile.lock: 0 source(s) pinned
```

`blue registry render --write` then writes each backend's publish workflow.
In blue's own distribution, a new package also needs a row in
`bidamas/NAMES.md`: the build is red without one. The full design is
[REGISTRY.md](docs/REGISTRY.md).

---

Source: `docs/CANONICAL-FORMS.md`

# Canonical forms

blue has one way to write each thing. This is the inventory of every place where
the surface accepts two or more spellings of one meaning, the spelling blue
writes, why, which layer of the compiler holds it, and the rule that names it.

## The principles, in order

1. **Readability first.** The canonical spelling is the one a person reading the
   line cold understands fastest: words over symbols where blue offers both,
   the descriptive name over the terse one, no clever shorthand. This decided
   every row marked *readability* below. **Amended 2026-10-27
   (`OPERATORS.md` §2):** universal notation is the readable spelling, so a
   symbol wins for indexing, ranges, membership and a science's own operators,
   when the corpus ranks the shape in its top tier or a discipline blue serves
   spells it that way. A rewrite whose safety needs a type fires only at a
   blueshift rung that knows the type; below it the long form stays canonical.
2. **One tree.** Two spellings of one meaning lower to one AST, so every tool
   (the evaluator, the VM, `def_hash`, the checker, the formatter, the LSP)
   sees one shape. Where two spellings built different trees with the same
   meaning, the parser or the resolver now builds the canonical tree.
3. **Corpus frequency** decides only what the first two leave open, measured
   with the parser over the 240 tracked `.b` files of pleme-io on 2026-10-19
   (blue, nix, arnes, substrate, ola-mundo, blackmatter-akeyless, makoto,
   nupastel), aggregated in DuckDB.

## How a rule is held

Every form below still **parses**: an older program, a model or a Ruby habit is
read and means exactly what it says. What it cannot do is stay in a stored
file:

| door | what happens to a non-canonical spelling |
|---|---|
| `blue fmt --write` | writes the canonical spelling |
| `blue run`, `blue test`, `blue check` | refuse a non-canonical entry naming the rules and `blue fmt --write x.b`; they never write a file (`BLUE_LAYOUT=rewrite` restores formatting in place). A loaded dependency is compiled as written: its form is judged by its producer (`BLUE_FORM`, `docs/COMPOUNDING.md`) |
| `blue fmt --check`, a bidama's form check | fail naming the file, the rules and the first place |
| `blue check`, the LSP | report each finding with its code; `blue check --fix` applies the fixes |
| a session, `blue eval`, a string | accepted as written: it has no canonical text to hold |

Two doors decide. The **form door** (`pipeline::form_diagnostics`) compares a
file with its canonical rendering; the parser records which accepted spelling
explains each difference (`blue_lang_syntax::spelling`). The **check stage**
holds what only resolution knows (a builtin's other name, a zero-parameter call)
and the refusals. `blue explain CODE` prints each row.

## The inventory

| written | canonical | why | layer | rule | fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `a && b`, `a \|\| b`, `!x`, `∧ ∨ ¬` | `a and b`, `a or b`, `not x` | readability: read aloud without a lookup; `!` vanishes beside a name. Corpus: 676 `&&`, 333 `\|\|`, 208 `!` | parser (one tree) | B0025 | autofix |
| `unless c` | `if not c` | readability: one conditional keyword; `unless … else` reads backwards. Corpus: 0 | parser | B0026 | autofix |
| `else` holding only `if … end` | `elsif` | one tree; a flat chain, one `end`. Corpus: 2 | parser, formatter | B0027 | autofix (kept when a comment sits beside the inner `if`) |
| `x.f(y)`, `x \|> f(y)` | `f(x, y)` | one tree; the function named first, a recursive call reads forwards. Corpus: 0, 0 | parser | B0028 | autofix |
| `{:a => 1}` | `{a: 1}` | one tree; reads as a field. Corpus: 0 (244 rockets with other keys stay) | parser | B0029 | autofix |
| `def f`, `fn … end` | `def f()`, `fn() … end` | one tree; the definition says it takes nothing | parser | B0030 | autofix |
| `not(x)`, `and(a, b)`, `mod(a, b)`, `equal?(a, b)`, `list(…)`, `define(x, v)`, `0 - x`, `≠ ≤ ≥ × ÷ − ≡` | `not x`, `a and b`, `a % b`, `a == b`, `[…]`, `x = v`, `-x`, the ASCII operator | one tree; readability: the operator a reader can type | parser | B0031 | autofix |
| `[1, 2,]`, `f(a,)`, `{a: 1,}`, `def f(a,)` | no trailing comma | was a parse error; now read and dropped, because models write it | parser | B0032 | autofix |
| `1000000`, `1_000`, `1e3`, a raw control or invisible character in a string | `1_000_000`, `1000`, `1000.0`, `"\u{1b}"` | readability: six or more digits grouped by threes; a character a reader cannot see is never in source (the formatter used to write a raw ESC byte). Corpus: 153 integers of 6+ digits, 6 raw control characters | formatter | B0033 | autofix |
| `not (a == b)`, `not (a != b)` | `a != b`, `a == b` | readability: one comparison; identical by okite D0002. Corpus: 9 | parser (builds `not=`) | B0034 | autofix |
| `{name: name}`, `{:name => name}` | `{name:}` | a label with no value takes the variable of the same name, so a map built from locals names each one once; `{name:, size: 3}` mixes with explicit values. Corpus: 201 entries in 33 files of blue (2026-10-22), 46 files rewritten | parser (reads `{name:}`, notes the long form) | B0046 | autofix |
| `"#{a}\n#{b}"`, `"done\n"`, `"\n"`: a `\n` escape in a string | `join_lines([a, b])`, `unlines(["done"])`, `line_break` | readability: a line break is seen, not counted in escapes; `join_lines` renders each element as interpolation does, so the text is the same (a differential of the old and new binaries, 2026-10-27, byte-identical). A string inside `quote` is data and keeps its escape; `@doc` example text is not rewritten. Corpus: 95 files of blue rewritten (2026-10-27) | parser (one tree) | B0065 | autofix |
| `get(m, :k)`, `get(m, "k")`, `nth(i, xs)`, `nth(0, xs)` | `m[:k]`, `m["k"]`, `xs[i]`, `xs[0]` | universal notation (principle 1, amended): indexing is read without a lookup. One tree: a keyword or string literal key is `get`, any other key `nth`, so a missing key and a position past either end are nil as before. `m.k` is not used for `get`: measured 2026-10-27, `blue-field` raises on a missing field (`errors.rs` `field`), `get` answers nil. A computed map key stays `get(m, k)`. Every bidama's tests byte-identical before and after (77 of 78; tsuiseki differs only in span timestamps and ids). Corpus: 101 files rewritten | parser (one tree) | B0066 | autofix |
| `nil?(x)`, `x == nil`, `nil == x` | `x.nil?` | readability: the test reads as a question put to the value, and one spelling replaces three. `x != nil` and `not x.nil?` stay: the opposite test is its own tree. Each form answers the same on every input class (`blue eval`, 2026-10-23); a map holding a `nil?` key answers `.nil?` with that key. Corpus: 7 `nil?`, the `== nil` tests of every bidama | parser (builds the field read), resolution (`nil?(x)`) | B0047 | autofix |
| `if c … else nil end`, an empty `else` | `if c … end` | an `if` that fails is already nil. Corpus: 85 | parser (drops the branch) | B0035 | autofix (kept when the `else` holds a comment) |
| `car`, `cdr`, `next`, `modulo`, `rem`, `bool?`, `comp`, `foldl`, `some?(x)`, `error_kind(e)`, `error_message(e)` | `first`, `rest`, `rest`, `a % b`, `a % b`, `boolean?`, `compose`, `reduce`, `x != nil`, `e.kind`, `e.message` | readability: the name a reader without Lisp knows; `some?` reads as "some element". Each pair measured equal on every input class (`blue eval`, 2026-10-19). Corpus: 2 `car`, 12 `cdr`, 34 `modulo`, 13 `foldl`, 2 `bool?`, 7 `nil?` | resolution | B0036 | autofix; writes `blue::first` where a listed import shadows the bare name |
| `throw(error(k, m))`, `throw(x)`, `try(x, catch(e(), h))`, `begin … end` as a whole `def` body | `raise(k, m)`, `raise(x)`, `x rescue h` or `begin … rescue e … end`, the clauses on the `def` | readability: one step to raise, a block that reads like Ruby's, the error a readable record. Corpus: 92 `throw(error(`, 178 `throw(`, 212 `try(` | resolution (`throw`), parser (`try`, `begin`) | B0037 | autofix |
| `apply(f, a, xs)` with `f` a name | `f(a, *xs)` | one tree; the call keeps its shape. Corpus: 41 | parser, formatter | B0042 | autofix |
| `(x) -> f(x)` with `f` a `def` of the file taking exactly those parameters | `f` | one function, the shorter name; `fn … end` on one line is B0024 | check stage | B0044 | autofix |
| `to_s(to_s(x))`, `string(trim(x))`, `to_int(to_int!(x))`, `to_float(sqrt(x))`, `trim(trim(x))`, `to_s("a")`: a conversion whose argument is a builtin call that already returns the kind it leaves alone, or a literal of that kind | the argument itself | the chain does nothing; one table, `blue_lang_check::chains::RULES`, read by the check stage, the formatter and the evaluator, each row carrying an okite law (D0013). `to_int(to_int(x))`, `to_float(to_float(x))` and `upcase(downcase(x))` stay: they change values. A local or definition named like the builtin is never rewritten | check stage, evaluator | B0045 | autofix |
| `if getenv("X_MAIN", "") == "1" … f … end` | `def main()`, called by `blue run` | one entry-point convention; no environment variable. Corpus: 8 | check stage | B0041 | autofix where the guard calls one zero-parameter function used nowhere else; refused otherwise |
| `ro_resolve_argv`, `ro_patch_argv`, `ro_main` in a program | `resolve_argv`, `patch_argv`, `main` | the file is the namespace; a prefix repeats it. Corpus: the nix programs and the `gen/` generators | check stage | B0043 | autofix where no stripped name is already used in the file or reserved; refused otherwise (a bidama's prefix is B0013/B0014) |
| `rescue e` with an empty or `nil` handler | `rescue _` and `nil`, or `x rescue nil` | silence must be visible | check stage | B0038 | refused |
| two tests with one name | distinct names | a failure must say which test | check stage | B0039 | refused |
| `retryCount` | `retry_count` | readability: one case for names. Corpus: 1 | check stage | B0040 | refused (a name is its callers' too) |
| whitespace, indentation, width 80, blank lines, redundant parentheses, a call whose one argument is a literal broken over lines | `blue fmt`'s layout | one layout; a short call stays on its line | formatter | B0024 | autofix |
| `name()` for a zero-parameter function | `name` | (shipped in v0.0.74) | resolution | B0023 | autofix |
| a `use` out of order, twice, or unread | sorted, once, read | (shipped) | check stage | B0015, B0016 | list sort and `use` form order: autofix; unused: refused |
| a bare name reached only through a bidama another `use` loaded; `retsu::first` with no `use("retsu")` | `use("retsu", [:first, :last])` added in package order; `use("retsu")` added | the file says what it reads | check stage | B0012, B0010 | autofix in a script (a bidama's Bluefile `needs` is the author's) |
| `blue::name` where the bare name is the builtin | `name` | (shipped) | resolution | B0018 | autofix |
| a `#` comment block documenting a `def`; a heredoc indented, with trailing spaces or edge blank lines; a blank line between `@doc` and its `def` | `@doc """` … `"""` at column 0 directly above the `def`; `@moduledoc` as the file's first form | documentation is a typed child of the definition, not a comment: it is in the tree, in `def_hash`, and its `expr #=> value` lines run as tests. The text is data (no escapes, no interpolation); its indentation is presentation, stripped at lex time. Corpus: 0 `@doc` before 2026-10-24 | parser (lexes the heredoc, builds `blue-doc`), formatter | B0024; B0056 lifts the `#` line | autofix |

## New forms these rules write

- **Logic words**: `and`, `or`, `not` are reserved. `not` binds as `!` did
  (tightly), and a negation that is an operand of a comparison or arithmetic is
  written `(not a) == b`.
- **Errors**: `raise(:kind, "message")`, `raise(:kind, "message", {data: d, cause: e})`,
  `raise(e)`. `x rescue fallback` binds loosest of all, below `|>`. A block:
  `begin … rescue :a, :b as e … rescue e … ensure … end`; a `def` takes the same
  clauses directly. An uncaught error prints `kind: message`, every cause, and
  the stack, and exits 1. The error value's fields: `e.kind`, `e.message`,
  `e.data`, `e.cause`, `e.trace` (the raise site, `file:line`); `"#{e}"` is
  `kind: message (at file:line)`.
- **Records**: `x.name` without parentheses reads a field: a map's keyword or
  string key, a keyed list (`exec_capture`'s `[[:status, n], …]`, a parsed JSON
  object), or an error's field. A missing field raises naming the fields there
  are; `get(m, :k)` reads a field that may be absent.
- **Splat**: `f(a, *xs)`, the list last.
- **Entry point**: `def main()`, called by `blue run` and by nothing else.
- **Libraries**: `deeta::json_at(doc, "spec.items.0.name")`, nil when any step
  is absent; `saishikou::retrying({times: 3, wait_ms: 500, on: [:timeout]}, fn() … end)`.

## Considered and not made rules

| forms | decision | why |
|---|---|---|
| `"a" + x` vs interpolation | no second form | `+` is numbers only; `"a#{x}"` is the one spelling |
| `concat(a, b)` vs `"#{a}#{b}"` | both stay | different trees, and `concat` is how a literal `#{` is built (222 calls) |
| `:sym` vs `"sym"` | both stay | different values |
| `x == true` vs `x` | both stay | different meanings under truthiness (2,479 in tests) |
| `eq?` vs `==`, `null?` vs `empty?`, `length` vs `count`, `some` vs `any?` | both stay | different answers on some input (`eq?` is identity; `null?("")`; `length(nil)` raises; `some` answers nil) |
| `count(x) == 0` vs `empty?(x)` | both stay | `count` raises where `empty?` answers; a rewrite would change a failure into a value |
| `if not c a else b end` vs `if c b else a end` | both stay | branch order is the author's emphasis, and swapping it moves comments |
| pipelines | call form | the tree does not remember the spelling; a pipeline rendering for long data-first chains needs a shape detector and is a formatter version bump (§V.13) |
| `def f()` vs `def f` | `def f()` | the definition says it takes nothing; only the call is bare |
| unused locals and parameters | B0002 stays a warning | renaming in flight would rename a parameter the author is about to use |
| `return`, `do`/braces blocks, `;`, `xs[i]` | one form already | refused by the parser with the canonical spelling named |
| a typed `raise :kind, "m"` keyword form | `raise(…)` call | blue has no paren-less calls; one call grammar |
| Result values and a `?` operator | not added | exceptions stay the one error model; `kyohi` holds refusals as data where a caller branches on them |
| retry as syntax (`retry`) | a bidama, `saishikou` | a bounded helper says its bound; a keyword hides a loop |
| a warning for rescuing a kind nothing raises | not built | no analysis can know which kinds a call raises |

---

Source: `docs/DIAGNOSTICS.md`

# Diagnostics

What blue's check stage reports, and the machine-readable shape of it.

Every rule lives in one registry, `blue_lang_check::RULES`
(`crates/blue-lang-check/src/rules.rs`). The check stage runs on every door —
`blue run`, `blue test`, `blue check`, the language server and every bidama
build — so an error-severity rule is a program that does not run or build.
`blue explain CODE` prints a rule's explanation and an example that violates
it; `blue explain --list` lists them.

## Codes

| code | slug | severity | law |
|---|---|---|---|
| B0001 | unbound-name | error | every name a program uses is bound |
| B0002 | unused-binding | warning | a local binding is read at least once, or its name starts with `_` |
| B0003 | return-type-mismatch | error | a typed definition's body produces its declared type |
| B0004 | operand-type-mismatch | error | an operator in a typed definition gets operands of its type |
| B0005 | argument-type-mismatch | error | a call to a typed definition passes the declared types |
| B0006 | syntax-error | error | a file parses |
| B0007 | malformed-waiver | error | a waiver names a known, waivable code and gives a reason |
| B0008 | unused-waiver | error | a waiver suppresses at least one diagnostic |
| B0009 | ambiguous-name | error | no two namespaces in one resolution tier define a name |
| B0010 | qualifier-not-imported | error | a qualified name's package is one the file `use`s |
| B0011 | no-such-definition | error | a qualified name, or a name a `use` lists, is a definition of that package |
| B0012 | implicit-reference | error | a bare name that is another bidama's definition is one the file lists, or is written qualified |
| B0013 | prefixed-definition | error | a bidama's definition does not spell its bidama |
| B0014 | mangled-namespace | error | a bidama does not prefix nine in ten of its definitions with one short `x_` |
| B0015 | non-canonical-import | error | a file's `use` forms come first, one per package, sorted, each list sorted |
| B0016 | unused-import | error | every `use` is reached, and every name it lists is read |
| B0017 | duplicate-definition | error | a namespace defines a function or macro once |
| B0018 | redundant-qualifier | error | a qualifier changes what its name means |
| B0019 | needs-mismatch | error | the bidamas a bidama `use`s are exactly the `needs` its Bluefile.lock records (`blue lock` derives them from the `use`s; a Bluefile `needs` row only narrows a range) |
| B0020 | package-as-value | error | a bidama's name is written as a qualifier, never as a value |
| B0021 | legacy-name | error | a renamed or moved definition is called by its new name; the old one is a bridge that closes at the next minor version |
| B0022 | legacy-misuse | error | a `legacy_names` declaration is one of each form per bidama, dated from a version it has reached, names no name twice, and moves a name only to a definition a loaded bidama holds |
| B0023 | bare-nullary-call | error | a call to a function that takes no parameters is written bare: `now_ms`, never `now_ms()` |
| B0024 | layout | error | a file is laid out as `blue fmt` writes it: indentation, line breaks at 80 columns, blank lines and parentheses |
| B0025 | logical-words | error | logic is written in words: `a and b`, `a or b`, `not x`, never `&&`, `\|\|`, `!` |
| B0026 | unless | error | a negated condition is written `if not c`, never `unless c` |
| B0027 | elsif | error | an `else` whose whole body is an `if` is written `elsif` |
| B0028 | call-form | error | a call is written `f(x, y)`: never `x.f(y)` or `x \|> f(y)` |
| B0029 | keyword-key | error | a map key that is a keyword is written `name: value`, never `:name => value` |
| B0030 | parameter-list | error | a definition and a lambda write their parameter list, even an empty one: `def f()`, `fn() … end` |
| B0031 | operator-spelling | error | an operator or literal is written as itself, never as the call it lowers to or a typographic alias |
| B0032 | trailing-comma | error | no comma before a closing bracket |
| B0033 | literal-spelling | error | a literal is written as `blue fmt` writes its value: digits of six or more grouped `1_000_000`, an invisible character escaped `\u{1b}` |
| B0034 | negated-comparison | error | a negated equality is written with the other operator: `a != b`, never `not (a == b)` |
| B0035 | else-nil | error | an `if` has no `else` whose body is empty or `nil` |
| B0036 | builtin-synonym | error | a builtin with two names is called by its readable one: `first` not `car`, `rest` not `cdr` or `next`, `a % b` not `modulo`/`rem`, `boolean?` not `bool?`, `compose` not `comp`, `reduce` not `foldl`, `x != nil` not `some?(x)`, `e.kind`/`e.message` not `error_kind`/`error_message` |
| B0037 | error-spelling | error | an error is raised with `raise` and caught with `rescue`: never `throw(error(…))` or `try(…, catch(…))` |
| B0038 | swallowed-error | error | a `rescue` that catches every error and does nothing names the error `_` |
| B0039 | duplicate-test-name | error | the tests of a file have distinct names |
| B0040 | identifier-case | error | a function, parameter or local is named in lower snake_case (`retry_count`, never `retryCount`); a top-level constant may be UPPER_SNAKE |
| B0041 | main-guard | error | a program's entry point is `def main()`, which `blue run` calls; never a top-level `if getenv("X_MAIN", "") == "1"` guard |
| B0042 | splat | error | a list passed as a call's last arguments is written `f(a, *xs)`, never `apply(f, a, xs)` with `f` a name |
| B0043 | prefixed-program | error | a program does not prefix every definition with one short `x_`: the file is the namespace |
| B0044 | eta-reduction | error | a function that only forwards its parameters to a named function is that name: `map(describe, vs)`, never `map((v) -> describe(v), vs)` |
| B0046 | map-pun | error | a map entry whose value is the variable of the same name is written `{name:}`, never `{name: name}` |
| B0047 | nil-test | error | a nil test is written `x.nil?`, never `nil?(x)`, `x == nil` or `nil == x` |
| B0045 | redundant-conversion | warning | a conversion is not applied to a value it leaves alone: `to_s(to_s(x))` is `to_s(x)`, never the longer chain |
| B0048 | undeclared-field-read | error | a fragment ref is read only for the fields its fragment declares; a parent never reads a child's field |
| B0049 | fragment-not-composed | error | a view's operation is the union of the fragments of the components it renders: a ref passed to a component comes from a selection that spreads its fragment, and every spread names a declared fragment |
| B0050 | field-not-in-schema | error | every fragment's type and field, and every `labels` enum and key, is in the frontend's schema |
| B0051 | enum-mirror | error | a literal list never mirrors an enum of the schema; display text is keyed by the enum with `labels` |
| B0052 | query-text | error | a view holds no GraphQL operation text; its operation is composed from fragments and sent by hash |
| B0053 | discarded-value | error | the value of a word that only returns a value is read: `assoc`, `append`, `to_s` and their kin are never a statement |
| B0056 | undocumented-definition | error | a bidama's public definition has a `@doc` whose first sentence starts with its name |
| B0057 | doc-without-example | error | a `@doc` holds at least one example, an indented `expr #=> value` line |
| B0058 | undocumented-bidama | error | a bidama's file opens with a `@moduledoc` holding its purpose and one whole example |
| B0059 | placeholder-doc | error | a `@doc` or `@moduledoc` says something: no empty text and no placeholder (`TODO`, `TBD`, `...`) |
| B0060 | restated-doc | error | a `@doc` never restates a type, a signature or a contract field: blue derives them |
| B0061 | undeclared-option | error | a function's option keys are a closed set: a call passes only keys the function reads, and a `checked(opts, [...])` list declares every key the function reads |
| B0062 | argument-kind | error | a value whose kind is known is never passed where a builtin, or the parameter it flows to, takes another kind |
| B0063 | nullary-as-function | error | a zero-argument definition passed where a function is taken is written `() -> name`; a bare zero-argument name is a call |
| B0064 | unformatted-producer | error | a program that writes a `.b` file writes it with `write_program`, which formats it; a producer owns the form of what it emits |
| B0065 | newline-escape | error | text of several lines is written as its lines: `join_lines([a, b])`, `unlines([a, b])` when it ends in a newline, `line_break` alone; never a `\n` escape in a string |
| B0066 | index | error | a key or position is read with brackets: `m[:k]` for `get(m, :k)`, `xs[i]` for `nth(i, xs)` |

The registry is the source of truth; a test fails if a code is missing here.

## Ratchets: how a rule becomes an error

A rule the corpus does not yet satisfy is registered with `ratchet: Some(n)`:
it is computed on every program and its findings are counted, not enforced.
`blue census [ROOT]` counts them over every `.b` file under ROOT, and
`checks.namespace-census` fails unless each count equals its row's ratchet
exactly, so every change to a count is a reviewed edit of the number. The
commit that brings a count to zero sets the row to `Some(0)`, and from then
on the rule is an error on every door. `blue census --findings` lists each
finding.

## The data laws (B0048–B0052)

The frontend's data laws (`theory/BLUE-FRONTEND.md` §2) are rows like every
other. A fragment declared with `danpen::fragment(:user_card, {on: "User",
fields: […]})` is the type `UserCard`; a parameter annotated with it holds a
fragment ref, and the typing ladder checks every read of it (B0048) and every
ref passed on to a component (B0049, whose fix adds the spread). The schema
enters through the project's Bluefile: `frontend(name, {views:, schema:})`
names the SDL, and the `generate(...)` whose inputs hold that SDL writes the
table the check reads (`danpen::render(sdl, :table)`), so
`checks.generated-<name>-fresh` keeps it current. A file under a frontend's
`views` is a view (B0052 applies); any other file of the project is checked
against the same table (B0050, B0051). A file with no frontend around it has
no table, and B0050–B0052 do not run for it. In nix a check program runs
alone in the store, so only `blue check`, the language server, `blue census`
and the corpus test read the table there.

`blue_lang_check::data_laws::Fragments` is the fragment and composition table
as data (each fragment's type, fields and spreads), for checks that build on
it.

## Name resolution order

A bare name resolves by tier, first match wins, deterministically
(`blue_lang_check::names::RESOLUTION_ORDER`): locals innermost first, then
the referencing file's own bidama (or, for a script, the file), then the
names the file lists in its `use` forms (`use("retsu", [:first])`), then
builtins (harness names, special forms, macros, values). A `use("x")` with no
list makes `x::name` reachable and no bare name; a bidama the file does not
`use` is not visible. Two namespaces in the tier that holds the name is B0009
(two lists naming it). A qualified name — `retsu::first`, or `blue::first`
for the builtin — bypasses the tiers and is exact.

The words the parser lowers its own syntax to (`blue_lang_syntax::LOWERED_HEADS`:
`list` for `[…]`, `concat` for interpolation, `not`, `and`, `or`, `mod`,
`equal?`, `not=`, `apply`) skip the own and listed tiers: a bare one is always
the builtin, so a bidama may define `list` and its literals still build lists.
Its own definition is reached qualified (`gitto::list`), and `B0018` does not
call that qualifier redundant. `get` is not among them: field access lowers to
`blue-field`, so a bidama may define `get` and use `x.name` freely.

The runtime evaluates the tree resolution produced: every definition keyed
`pkg/name` (`%root/name` for a script), every reference to it as that key, a
builtin bare. So the runtime binds exactly what the check resolved.

## Overrides, and `blue explain-name`

When a bare name is bound in one tier while a lower tier also holds it — a
bidama's own `count` over the builtin, a listed `first` over the builtin — the
higher tier wins; that is the order, not an error, since each tier is
something the author wrote. `blue check --format json` records each one in
the entry file as a line after the diagnostics:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `kind` | `override` |
| `name` | the name as written |
| location fields | where the reference is |
| `tier` | the tier that won: `own` or `imported` |
| `namespace` | the winning namespace: a bidama's name, or `this file` |
| `shadowed` | each lower-tier candidate, as `{tier, namespace}` |

`blue explain-name NAME FILE:LINE` prints the whole path for one name at one
place: each tier, what it holds, and which wins.

## Waivers

The one escape hatch is a comment directly above a top-level definition:

```
# waive B0002: the callback shape is fixed
def on_event(event, ctx)
  event
end
```

It suppresses that code inside that definition and nowhere else. There is no
file-wide or global waiver. A waived diagnostic is still reported: `blue check`
counts it, and `--format json` lists it with its `waiver` set.

## `blue check --format json`

JSON Lines on stdout: one object per diagnostic per line, reported ones first,
then waived ones. The exit status is 1 when any error-severity diagnostic is
reported. The field names below are stable; `crates/blue-lang-cli/tests/check_json.rs`
pins the exact output and fails if a field here is undocumented.

| field | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `code` | string | the rule, `B0001` |
| `slug` | string | the rule's kebab-case name, `unbound-name` |
| `severity` | string | `error` or `warning` |
| `message` | string | what is wrong, one line |
| `file` | string or null | the file the primary span is in (an imported bidama's own path when the fault is there) |
| `line`, `column` | number or null | start, 1-based; columns count characters, not bytes |
| `end_line`, `end_column` | number or null | end (exclusive), same units |
| `byte_start`, `byte_end` | number or null | the half-open byte range in `file` |
| `help` | string or null | one line on what to do |
| `related` | array | other places: each has the location fields above and a `message` |
| `fixes` | array | suggested repairs, best first |
| `waiver` | object or null | set when a waiver suppressed this diagnostic: `reason`, and the waiver's `line` |

Each entry of `fixes`:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `message` | what the fix does, `replace with \`length\` (builtin)` |
| `applicability` | `machine-applicable` (preserves meaning; `--fix` applies it) or `maybe-incorrect` (a guess; never applied automatically) |
| `edits` | byte-range replacements applied together: the location fields, `original` (what the range must still contain, or the edit is refused) and `replacement` |

A location is `null` throughout when it cannot be placed honestly (for
example, a span that is not a range in the named file).

## `blue run --format json`

A runtime error as one JSON object on stdout, the same error `blue run` prints
as text: `stage` (`eval`), `severity`, `message` (names as the author writes
them), `file`, `line`, `column` (each `null` when it cannot be justified), and
`stack`, the blue call stack innermost first, each frame `function`, `file`,
`line`, `column`, or `builtin: true` for a builtin the runtime defines in
tatara-lisp. The last frame is `<top level>` when the whole stack was
recorded; `stack_depth` counts every frame unwound, recorded or not (a trace
keeps 256). Any other stage's error is `stage` (`parse`, `check`, `import`)
and `message`. `crates/blue-lang-cli/tests/observe.rs` pins the shape.

## `blue check --fix`

Applies every machine-applicable fix whose edits land in the named file and
still match their `original`, skips overlapping ones, then re-formats and
re-checks the file and reports what remains. Suggestions marked
`maybe-incorrect` are never applied.

`blue check --fix --only CODE FILE` (repeatable) applies only those codes'
fixes, to the file as written: no re-format, no project-rule fix, no Bluefile
edit. A project pinned to an older blue takes one rule's fix from a newer blue
this way, then formats with its own (`blue fmt --write`).

## Project rules

A project adds its own check rules, written in blue, by naming them in its
Bluefile:

```
rule("R0001", "rules/conventions.b", "nil_predicate")
rule("R0002", "rules/conventions.b", "loud_call", "warning")
```

`rule(code, file, def[, severity])` names a definition in a blue file (relative
to the Bluefile). `blue check FILE` gathers the rules of every Bluefile in
FILE's directory and its ancestors, up to the directory holding `.git`, and
calls each one on every top-level form of FILE, beside the registry. A code
declared by two Bluefiles is refused.

**Codes.** A project code is one to four capital letters, never `B` alone,
then four digits (`R0001`, `KZ0003`). `B` + four digits is blue's registry, so
the two never meet. Severity is `error` (the default) or `warning`.

**The ABI.** The definition takes one argument, a top-level form as data (the
tree the parser wrote, as a macro sees its arguments: symbols, lists, `quote`
as `(quote x)`), and returns a list of findings. A finding is a map:

| key | | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `at` | required | the path to the node, one child index per level; `[]` is the form itself |
| `message` | required | a string |
| `help` | optional | a string |
| `fix` | optional | a tree that replaces the node at `at`, usually built with `quote … unquote(x) … end` |

```
def nil_predicate(form)
  hits = filter(fn(p) call?(last(p), "nil?", 1) end, nodes(form, []))
  map(
    fn(p)
      arg = nth(1, last(p))
      {at: first(p), message: "write `x.nil?`", fix: quote
        unquote(arg).nil?
      end}
    end,
    hits
  )
end
```

The code and severity are the Bluefile row's. A path, not a byte offset: the
rule sees only data, and `blue check` resolves the path against the form it
gave the rule, so the rule needs no access to the source (and can later run as
a wasm module, `theory/BLUE-EXECUTION.md` §I.2). A fix is rendered by the
formatter and proved before `--fix` will apply it: the edited file is parsed
and must hold exactly the rule's tree at that path (the rendering is retried in
parentheses when an operator binds differently in place); otherwise it is
offered as `maybe-incorrect`.

**The frame.** A rule program, imported bidamas included, may name every
builtin except the host effects (process, filesystem, environment, clock,
network), printing, and `eval`, `require` and `provide`. A rule that names one
is refused before it runs. Each call runs under a step budget
(`blue_lang_runtime::project_rules::RULE_STEPS`).

**Failures.** A rule that does not load, reaches outside its frame, raises,
runs past its budget, or returns anything but a list of findings is reported
once, as an error under its code with the slug `rule-failure`, and is not run
on the file's remaining forms. The other rules still report.

**Waivers** use the one grammar: `# waive R0001: reason` above the definition.
The check stage that `blue run`, `blue test` and every build run does not run
project rules, so it leaves a project-code waiver alone; `blue check` reports
one that names no declared rule (B0007) or suppresses nothing (B0008).

**Output.** Findings are diagnostics in every format above: `file:line:col:
error[R0001]: message`, the same JSON object (the slug is the definition's
name, kebab-cased), the same `fixes`. `blue check` prints `project rules: N`
when any apply.

**In nix**, a project whose Bluefile declares rules gets
`checks.project-rules-hold`: `blue check` on every `.b` file of its packages and
every run, check and app program.

## `blue ast --resolved --json`

How every name in a file resolves, under both rules: today's **flat** rule
(one global environment; the definition evaluated last wins, a builtin only
when no program form defines the name) and **per-bidama namespaces** (locals,
then the file's own package, then its explicit imports, then builtins; a
qualified name exactly). One JSON object on stdout.
`crates/blue-lang-cli/tests/ast_resolved.rs` pins the exact output and fails
if a field here is undocumented. A migration is proven on it: a program whose
`flat` and `ns` trees are equal means the same thing under either rule.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `namespace` | the entry file's bidama (from the Bluefile beside it), or `null` for the root namespace |
| `flat` | the entry file's top-level forms, resolved under the flat rule: each definition renamed to its runtime key (`retsu/first`; `%root/f` for a script) and each reference to what the rule binds it to (a builtin stays bare) |
| `ns` | the same forms under per-bidama namespaces |
| `references` | every non-local reference in the entry file |
| `imports` | the entry file's `use` declarations: the location fields, `package`, and `names` (the list, empty for a whole-package `use`) |
| `first_line` | the first line of the entry file's first top-level form, or `null` |
| `definitions` | the entry file's top-level definitions: the location fields and `name` |
| `builtins` | every name the interpreter binds, sorted |
| `reserved` | the reserved words, which no definition can be named |

Each entry of `references` carries the location fields of `blue check` and:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `top_level` | the index of the top-level form it is in |
| `written` | the symbol as the tree has it: `first`, or `retsu/first` for `retsu::first` |
| `opaque` | inside a macro call's arguments |
| `flat`, `ns` | what each rule binds it to |
| `locals` | the locals in scope where it is written, innermost first |
| `position` | `call` (the head of a call), `value` (anywhere else in code), `place` (the name `set!` rebinds) or `syntax` (a macro head, a template symbol) |
| `argc` | for a `call`, how many arguments it passes; `null` otherwise |
| `nullary` | what `ns` binds it to takes exactly zero parameters: a bare `value` reference is CALLED, and a `call` with `argc` 0 is B0023 |

This list is how a definition's callers are found: bare calls have no
parentheses, so searching the text for `name(` misses every one.

A binding (`flat`, `ns`) has:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `kind` | `def` (a program definition), `builtin`, `local`, `ambiguous` (two imports list it) or `unbound` |
| `namespace` | the defining bidama for a `def`; `null` otherwise, and for the root namespace |
| `name` | the definition's or builtin's name |
| `key` | the symbol the resolved tree writes, or `null` when it keeps the written one |

---

Source: `docs/SAFETY.md`

# Safety first: blue's posture, row by row

Operator, 2026-10-24: *"the default posture for bluelang and blue scripting is
safety first, fully leveraging rust based safety"*.

This document turns that sentence into a matrix. Each row is one guarantee
that Rust gives. Each row says what blue does today (measured, with
`file:line`), the gap, the gate that closes it, the seal tier, and the
default with its off switch. A gate is on by default. An off switch is
explicit and local. Behaviour is configured off, never deleted.

## 1. Destination

Every blue program and every blue script is safe by default. A bad state is
refused at the earliest door that can see it: the parser, then the check
stage, then the runtime. Every effect outside the program is a declared
capability, granted at the root and narrowed for each script, each bidama and
each process. Nothing a program does can corrupt memory, race on shared
state or abort the process: Rust under the runtime is the trusted base, and
the base has one audited `unsafe` seam per foreign ABI. A script gets the same
gates as a project. An unsafe operation is possible, but it is written down,
named in the file and visible to a reader and to `blue check`.

World-facts that limit this destination:

- WASI has no subprocess spawn at any preview level. `Process` has no WASI
  lowering (`crates/blue-lang-waku/src/capability.rs:110`).
- A Linux shebang passes everything after the interpreter as ONE argument.
  A script that declares flags in its shebang needs `env -S` (coreutils 8.30
  and later, and macOS `env`).
- A dynamic language cannot prove purity of a higher-order call without an
  effect system. `map(f, xs)` may write if `f` writes.
- A Rust panic in a native function unwinds through the evaluator. A
  `panic = "abort"` profile would make it uncatchable. The workspace sets no
  `panic` profile today (`Cargo.toml`), so it unwinds.

Every other limit in this document is phrased in blue's own abstractions, so
it is ours to dissolve (MIRAGEM).

## 2. Ground: what exists

Measured on `origin/main` at `6f1bb37` (2026-10-24), plus the two gates this
document lands.

- **One check stage on every door.** `run`, `test`, `check`, the hosted loader
  and every bidama build call `check_stage`
  (`crates/blue-lang-runtime/src/pipeline.rs:458`). An error-severity rule
  stops a program before it runs. 53 B-codes exist (`docs/DIAGNOSTICS.md`).
- **A closed capability set.** `blue_lang_waku::Capability` has six host
  effects: process, filesystem, environment, clock, network, entropy
  (`crates/blue-lang-waku/src/capability.rs:116-137`,
  `host_effects` at `:428`). The set has no `Other(String)` arm.
- **Pure sessions.** `blue eval`, `repl` and `serve` bind every ungranted host
  name to a refusal (`crates/blue-lang-runtime/src/session.rs:744`).
  `--allow` widens the frame. A process the session spawns gets the same
  frame (`crates/blue-lang-runtime/src/lib.rs:138`).
- **Ambient `blue run`.** Before this document, `blue run` and `blue FILE`
  installed the whole `sys` layer (`lib.rs:114`) with no frame. A script
  reached every host capability.
- **Bounds.** Call depth 100 000 (`ExecutionBounds::DEFAULT`, `lib.rs:249`),
  refused as a catchable error. Parse depth 256
  (`crates/blue-lang-syntax/src/parse.rs:688`). Steps unbounded by default;
  sessions take `--budget`; project rules run under 10 000 000 steps
  (`crates/blue-lang-runtime/src/project_rules.rs:53`).
- **Share-nothing processes.** Each process owns its interpreter. A message is
  deep-copied, and a function or host handle is refused on send
  (`crates/blue-lang-proc/src/mailbox.rs:130`, `:215`).
- **Unsafe Rust.** 18 crates. Four hold `unsafe` in non-test code:
  `blue-lang-kiwari` (59 occurrences, one seam,
  `src/lib.rs:18` `#![deny(unsafe_code)]`, `src/ts.rs:13` the one
  `#[allow]`, `tests/seam.rs` the gate), `blue-lang-runtime`
  (`src/alloc.rs:114`, the counting `GlobalAlloc`), `blue-lang-wasm` (three
  `extern "C"` exports, `src/lib.rs:76,84,123`) and `blue-lang-cli`
  (`src/repl.rs:340`, the SIGINT handler, under a module `deny`). No
  workspace `[lints]` table exists. Only kiwari denies `unsafe_code` at its
  crate root, so 17 of 18 crates accept a new `unsafe` block silently.
- **Absence.** Another agent writes `docs/ABSENCE.md` (an `Option` bidama and
  a nil checker rule) in parallel. This document points at it and does not
  redesign it.

## 3. Research: Rust's guarantees, adopted or adapted

| Rust mechanism | blue's decision | why |
|---|---|---|
| `Option<T>`, no null | adapt: `docs/ABSENCE.md` | blue has `nil`; the Option bidama and its rule own the row |
| `Result` + `#[must_use]` | adapt: refusals as data (`kyohi`), B0038, B0053 | blue raises; a dropped value is the must-use bug |
| exhaustive `match` | adapt: a closed-set `case` rule | blue's `case` compares with `==` and has no enum type yet |
| immutable by default | adopt: persistent values | already true of every blue value |
| `&mut` uniqueness | skip | no blue value is mutable, so there is nothing to alias |
| bounds-checked index | adopt (memory) / adapt (semantics) | `nth` out of range is `nil`, so the semantic row is absence |
| checked overflow (debug) | adopt | every integer operator raises on overflow |
| no implicit coercion | adopt for operators, adapt for calls | gradual types check typed regions only |
| `unsafe` blocks | adapt: capabilities | a blue program has no raw memory; its "unsafe" is host effect |
| `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` | adopt for blue's own crates | one seam per foreign ABI, like kiwari |
| `Send` / `Sync` | adopt as share-nothing | processes copy; handles and functions refuse to cross |
| panic vs `Result` | adapt | a fault is a typed, catchable refusal, never an abort |
| `Cargo.lock` + checksums | adapt: `Bluefile.lock` | records ranges and source NAR hashes, not bidama content |
| `secrecy` crate (ecosystem) | adapt | a secret is an opaque value read from a file |
| `Command::arg` / bound SQL params | adopt | `exec_*` has no shell; `pg_query` binds `$1…` |

## 4. The matrix

Tiers, weakest to strongest: **open** (no gate), **runtime-refused**,
**checked-at-expansion**, **parse-rejected**, **unrepresentable**. A cell
reads "today → after the gate". ✅ marks a row already sealed at its target
tier. ⚠️ marks a partial seal. ❌ marks an open row.

| # | Guarantee | blue today | Gate | Tier today → target | Default (off switch) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | No null | ❌ `nil` everywhere; `nth`, `get`, `to_int` answer `nil` | `docs/ABSENCE.md`: Option bidama + nil rule | open → checked-at-expansion | on (`# waive <code>`) |
| 2 | Must-use results | ⚠️ B0038 swallowed-error; **B0053 discarded-value (landed)** | B0053 for first-order words; a refusal-list rule next | checked-at-expansion | on (`# waive B0053: reason`) |
| 3 | Exhaustive match | ❌ `case` falls through to `nil` | closed-set `case` rule | open → checked-at-expansion | on (`else` arm, or waive) |
| 4 | Immutability, no aliasing | ✅ values are persistent; `set!` rebinds a name, never a value | none needed | unrepresentable | n/a |
| 5 | Bounds-checked indexing | ✅ memory: no raw index exists; ⚠️ semantics: `nth` out of range is `nil` | row 1 owns the `nil` | unrepresentable (memory) | n/a |
| 6 | Integer overflow, numeric conversion | ✅ `+ - * abs floor` raise on overflow; `/` by zero raises; `to_int` of a huge float is `nil` | `to_int` → row 1 | runtime-refused | on, no off |
| 7 | No implicit coercion | ⚠️ operators refuse mixed types; `4 == 4.0` is true; call types are checked only inside typed definitions (B0003–B0005) | call-site checks from any caller when the argument is a literal | runtime-refused → checked-at-expansion | on |
| 8 | `unsafe` ⇔ declared capability | ⚠️ sessions pure by default; **`blue run --allow` and shebang `--allow` (landed)**; an undeclared run is still ambient | default flip for scripts, then `posture(reach:)` for bidamas | checked-at-expansion (entry) + runtime-refused (bidama, process) | declared: on; undeclared: ambient until phase 3 (`--allow host`) |
| 9 | Memory safety of the host seam | ⚠️ 1 of 18 crates denies `unsafe_code` at its root | workspace `unsafe_code = "deny"`, one `#[allow]` per seam, one seam test | unrepresentable for kiwari → unrepresentable for every crate | on (`#[allow(unsafe_code)]` at a named seam) |
| 10 | No data races | ✅ share-nothing processes; copy on send; handles refuse to cross | none needed | unrepresentable | n/a |
| 11 | Panic vs typed refusal | ⚠️ blue faults are catchable; a Rust panic in a native function is not a blue error | one unwind seam at the native-call boundary → `:internal` refusal | open → runtime-refused | on |
| 12 | Resource bounds | ⚠️ depth bounded; steps unbounded by default; no memory or wall-clock bound | `max_alloc_bytes`, `max_wall_ms` bounds; on for doors that run code they did not write | runtime-refused | off for `run` (it removes working behaviour), on for sessions and rules |
| 13 | Supply chain | ⚠️ `Bluefile.lock` holds `bluefile_b3`, version ranges and source NAR hashes; B0019 needs-mismatch | the lock records each resolved bidama's b3; the loader refuses a mismatch | runtime-refused at load | on (`blue lock` rewrites) |
| 14 | Secrets | ❌ a secret is a plain string; `pg_connect` takes a password in the URL | a secret bidama (named through `naming`): read from a file, opaque, redacted on print, refused on send | open → unrepresentable (print) + checked-at-expansion (literal) | on (`# waive`) |
| 15 | Injection | ⚠️ `exec_*` has no shell; `pg_query` binds params; `sh_exec` and `pg_execute` take text | rule: `sh_exec` / `pg_execute` with an interpolated argument | checked-at-expansion | on (`# waive`) |
| 16 | Blue scripting parity | ⚠️ a script gets the check stage's errors; no warnings, no project rules, ambient capabilities | shebang `--allow` (landed); project rules on `run`; default flip | checked-at-expansion | on |
| 17 | Module privacy: a package cannot rebind a name outside itself | ✅ runtime: definitions keyed `pkg/name`; ✅ check: a bidama definition never changes an importer's bare builtin call (B0012 only for listed flat-era names, inside their window) | `docs/NAMESPACES.md` | unrepresentable (runtime) + checked-at-expansion | on, no off; the flat-era refusal goes off per name when its `legacy_names` window closes |
| 18 | Session-mistake hard blocks | ✅ B0061 undeclared-option, B0062 argument-kind, B0063 nullary-as-function, B0064 unformatted-producer (`write_program`); ✅ `gen/retired.b`: a retired word ships its `legacy_names` fixer (prepush); ✅ `blue test` scrubs the inherited git environment and writes only under the temporary root | registry witnesses, spec rows `safety.B0061*`–`safety.B0064*`, `crates/blue-lang-cli/tests/hermetic.rs` | checked-at-expansion (codes), runtime-refused (test writes) | on; `# waive <code>: reason`; `BLUE_TEST_ENV=inherit`, `BLUE_TEST_WRITES=anywhere` |

**Count:** 16 rows. Sealed at their target tier today: 4 (rows 4, 5, 6,
10; row 5 for memory, its `nil` half belongs to row 1). Partly sealed: 9
(rows 2, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16). Open: 3 (rows 1, 3, 14).

**Rows in flight with other owners.** Each owner adds its own row here, with
the same columns, when its gate lands. This document does not land them.

- Namespace leaks: a bidama definition that shadows a builtin (the measured
  case: a package `def` shadowed `read`).
- Build hygiene: generated-file conflicts, gate speed, `gen` version skew,
  formatter drift across consumers.

## 5. Row notes (measurements)

**Row 1, null.** `nth(5, [1, 2])` is `nil`, `get({a: 1}, :b)` is `nil`,
`to_int("12x")` is `nil`; built-in `first([])` raises. B0047 fixes the nil
test spelling only. The design and the rule are `docs/ABSENCE.md`.

**Row 2, must-use.** blue raises errors, so the `Result` that Rust drops does
not exist as a value. Two must-use bugs remain. A catch-all that ignores its
error is B0038 (`crates/blue-lang-check/src/form_rules.rs:212`). A call to a
word that only returns a value, written as a statement, is dead: blue values
do not change, so `assoc(m, :a, 1)` alone on a line does nothing. B0053
(`form_rules.rs:283`, registry `rules.rs:1082`) refuses it for 23 first-order
words. `map`, `filter` and `reduce` are excluded: their function may write.
Census at landing: 0 hits in 355 `.b` files, so no ratchet. A refusal list
from `kyohi::check` that nobody reads is the next case.

**Row 3, exhaustive match.** `case v when 1 … end` with no matching arm is
`nil` (measured). `match` (tatara) has no blue spelling. The gate needs a
closed set to be exhaustive over: a `model(...)` enum, the kyohi ledger
kinds, or a keyword list the file declares. The rule then refuses a `case`
over that set that misses a member and has no `else`.

**Row 4, immutability.** `ys = xs; ys = append(ys, [2])` leaves `xs` as `[1]`
(measured). `set!` rebinds a name, and a name a forked process inherited is
sealed and refuses it (`docs/REFERENCE.md`, `set!`). There is no mutable
blue value, so aliasing has nothing to break. Channels and host handles are
the only stateful values, and row 10 keeps them inside one process.

**Row 6, numbers.** Measured: `9223372036854775807 + 1` raises "integer
overflow in `+`"; `* 2` and `abs(min)` raise the same way; `floor(9.9e300)`
raises; `1 / 0` and `1.0 / 0` raise "division by zero" (stricter than IEEE
754); `to_int(1.0e300)` is `nil`. Decision: keep checked arithmetic, never
wrap and never promote to a bignum.

**Row 7, coercion.** Measured: `"a" + 1`, `1 + "a"`, `"a" + "b"` and
`1 < "a"` raise a type mismatch; `1 == "1"` is false; `4 == 4.0` is true
(numeric equality crosses Int and Float); truthiness is Ruby's (`0`, `""`
and `[]` are true). A typed definition called with a string from an untyped
`main` fails at run time, not at check time: B0005 checks a call only inside
a typed caller.

**Row 8, capabilities.** The landed gate: `blue run --allow CAP` and
`blue --allow CAP FILE` (`crates/blue-lang-cli/src/script.rs:36`,
`repl.rs:46`). `CAP` is `none`, `host`, or one label. With the flag, the run
builds the session frame (`session::frame_granting`) and
`pipeline::run_framed` (`pipeline.rs:194`) does two things. First, a host
name the entry file writes outside the frame stops the program before
anything runs (`entry_escapes`, `pipeline.rs:229`). Second, every ungranted
host name is bound to a refusal (`lib.rs:161`), so a bidama or a spawned
process that reaches it is refused where it calls it. Without the flag the
run is ambient, as before. Two gaps stay open. A refusal is a normal error,
so `rescue _` can swallow it (measured in
`crates/blue-lang-cli/tests/allow.rs`). And a bidama cannot yet declare its
own reach: `posture` takes only `when`
(`crates/blue-lang-pkg/src/bluefile.rs:76`).

**Row 9, host memory.** blue has no pointer and no raw buffer; all memory is
Rust's. The four seams are listed in §2. The gate is one workspace lint table
plus `#[allow(unsafe_code)]` at each seam and a test like kiwari's
`tests/seam.rs`, so a new `unsafe` anywhere is a compile error.

**Row 10, races.** Each process owns its `Vm` and its `Interpreter`; a
message is deep-copied; a function or host handle is refused on send
(`crates/blue-lang-proc/src/lib.rs`, `mailbox.rs:130,215`). Host threads
(`net/serve.rs`, `session/protocol.rs`) are Rust, so Rust's `Send` and `Sync`
check them.

**Row 11, panics.** blue faults (depth, fuel, type, overflow, a raise) are
catchable and typed. `catch_unwind` appears only in `blue-lang-syntax` tests
(totality). A panic in a native function therefore ends the run with a Rust
message, not a blue error with a kind.

**Row 12, resources.** Call depth refuses at 100 000 (measured: "call depth
budget of 100000 exceeded in `r`"). Steps are unbounded on `run` on purpose
(`lib.rs:241-251`: a default step bound removed working simulations). The
counting allocator (`alloc.rs`) measures for `blue profile`; nothing bounds
memory or time.

**Row 13, supply chain.** `Bluefile.lock` records `bluefile_b3` and each
source's NAR hash (`crates/blue-lang-pkg/src/lock.rs:118,127`), and a bidama's
`needs` as version ranges. The load path skips a copy whose version is
outside the locked range. Two copies at the same version with different
content are not told apart.

**Row 14, secrets.** No secret type exists. `pg_connect` takes a password in
the URL's userinfo. `ed25519_keypair` returns the secret as hex text. kensa's
Rust side reads `password_file` and refuses a literal; blue has no such
word.

**Row 15, injection.** `exec_capture`, `exec_check`, `exec_ok?` and the
`exec_with_*` words call `Command::new(cmd)` with an argument vector and no
shell. `sh_exec` runs `sh -c TEXT` (`crates/blue-lang-runtime/src/sys.rs:208`).
`pg_query` sends `$1…` parameters (`net/pg.rs:163`); `pg_execute` sends text
(`net/pg.rs:200`). `http_request` refuses `https`. `path_join` does not refuse
`..`.

**Row 16, scripts.** `blue FILE` is `blue run --quiet FILE` (`script.rs`), so a
script gets every error-severity rule of the check stage, exactly as a
project does. Compared with `blue check`, a script run does not print
warnings (B0002, B0045), does not run the project's `rule(...)` rows, and
does not check `test` blocks (`Checking::WithTests`, `pipeline.rs:1208`).
Before this document a script also had every host capability with no way to
say less. Now the shebang states it:

```text
#!/usr/bin/env -S blue --allow filesystem --allow environment
```

## 6. States and trust

A run is in one of these capability states:

- **ambient**: no `--allow`. Every host capability. Today's default.
- **declared**: `--allow` names a set. The frame is that set.
- **refused-before-run**: the entry file writes a name outside the frame. No
  effect has happened.
- **refused-at-call**: a bidama or a process reaches a name outside the
  frame. Effects before the call have happened.
- **unknown capability**: `--allow disk`. The CLI refuses the flag and names
  the legal values.

Trust: the root (the person or the nix wrapper that starts `blue`) grants
capabilities. A script narrows them in its own shebang. A bidama cannot
widen them. A spawned process inherits the frame and cannot widen it
(`Waku::narrow` has no widening method).

## 7. Diagrams

The layers, with the trusted base at the bottom:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph S["script / program (.b)"]
    SB["shebang: blue --allow CAP"]
    SRC["source"]
  end
  subgraph B["bidamas"]
    KY["kyohi: refusals as data"]
    OPT["Option bidama (ABSENCE.md)"]
    SEC["secret bidama (row 14, design)"]
  end
  subgraph C["checker (blue-lang-check)"]
    RULES["RULES registry: B0001..B0060"]
    REACH["entry reach check (run_framed)"]
  end
  subgraph R["runtime (blue-lang-runtime, blue-lang-proc)"]
    FRAME["frame: ungranted host names bound to refusals"]
    BOUNDS["bounds: depth, steps"]
    PROC["share-nothing processes"]
  end
  subgraph H["Rust host: the trusted base"]
    SYS["sys layer: six host capabilities"]
    SEAMS["unsafe seams: kiwari, alloc, wasm, sigint"]
  end
  SB --> REACH
  SRC --> RULES
  SRC --> REACH
  B --> RULES
  RULES --> FRAME
  REACH --> FRAME
  FRAME --> SYS
  PROC --> FRAME
  BOUNDS --> PROC
  SYS --> SEAMS
```

A script run with a declared capability:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant OS
  participant CLI as blue CLI
  participant P as pipeline
  participant I as interpreter
  OS->>CLI: tool.b via env -S blue --allow filesystem
  CLI->>CLI: route: run --quiet --allow filesystem tool.b
  CLI->>P: run_framed(entry, frame = {filesystem})
  P->>P: parse, resolve uses, check stage (B-codes)
  P->>P: entry_escapes: host names outside the frame
  alt the entry writes getenv
    P-->>CLI: refused before run (environment)
  else clean entry
    P->>I: bind ungranted host names to refusals
    I->>I: run main
    I-->>CLI: a bidama reaches exec_capture: refused at call
  end
```

The capability lifecycle of one script:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> ambient: no --allow
  [*] --> declared: --allow CAP
  [*] --> unknown: --allow disk
  unknown --> [*]: CLI refuses the flag
  declared --> refused_before_run: entry writes an ungranted name
  declared --> running: entry is clean
  running --> refused_at_call: bidama or process reaches an ungranted name
  running --> done
  ambient --> done
  refused_before_run --> [*]
  refused_at_call --> [*]
  done --> [*]
```

## 8. Decisions

**D1. Where a script declares its capabilities: the shebang, as `--allow`.**
One spelling for the CLI and the script; the reader sees it on line 1.
Rejected: an in-file `capabilities(...)` form (a second declaration path and
a manifest word inside program code; it can come later as sugar that lowers
to the same frame). Rejected: an environment variable (invisible in the file,
and ambient for every child).

**D2. Static check over the entry file, runtime refusal for the rest.**
The entry file is what the author wrote, so a host name there is refused
before any effect. Rejected: the static check over the whole resolved
program. It refuses a pure use of a bidama that holds an unrelated host word,
which is collateral scope (UNREPRESENTABILITY §II.2.1).

**D3. The default for an undeclared script stays ambient now.** Rejected:
pure by default today. Every working script that reads a file would stop, so
